prompt: What does it mean for a problem to be NP-hard but not necessarily in NP?
options: It's easier than NP-complete problems
Every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time, but its own solutions may not be verifiable in polynomial time
It has already been proven unsolvable
It is automatically also in P
explanation: NP-hard only requires being 'at least as hard as' every NP problem via reduction — it doesn't require membership in NP itself. NP-complete = NP-hard AND in NP.

prompt: What is the standard two-step approach to prove a new problem X is NP-complete?
acceptedAnswers: show x is in np and reduce a known np-complete problem to x
prove np membership and reduce from a known np-complete problem
explanation: 1) Show X ∈ NP (a solution can be checked in poly time). 2) Show a known NP-complete problem reduces to X in poly time.

prompt: Which pair correctly matches (polynomial-time problem, NP-complete problem)?
options: 2-colorability (bipartiteness) is in P; 3-colorability is NP-complete
3-colorability is in P; 2-colorability is NP-complete
Both 2-colorability and 3-colorability are in P
Both 2-colorability and 3-colorability are NP-complete
explanation: 2-colorability (bipartiteness) is checkable via BFS/DFS in O(V+E) — a vertex's color deterministically forces its neighbors' colors. 3-colorability leaves 2 open options per neighbor, creating exponential branching, and is one of Karp's original 21 NP-complete problems.

options: 2-SAT is in P (solvable via implication graphs and SCCs); 3-SAT is NP-complete
Both are NP-complete
Both are in P
3-SAT is in P; 2-SAT is NP-complete
explanation: 2-literal clauses encode pairwise implications decidable via a graph-connectivity (SCC) check. 3-literal clauses interlink variables in a way that resists this shortcut — 3-SAT is the canonical NP-complete problem.

prompt: Fill in the blank from the standard P/NP text: an entscheidungsproblem L_E belongs to the class P exactly when there is an algorithm solving it deterministically in ___-case ___ time.
explanation: P requires a deterministic algorithm with polynomial WORST-CASE runtime — not merely average-case or best-case polynomial.

prompt: What is the canonical NP-complete problem that most NP-completeness proofs ultimately chain their reduction back to (proven directly via the Cook-Levin theorem)?
explanation: SAT (and its restricted form 3SAT) is proven NP-complete directly by encoding a poly-time verifier's entire computation as a boolean formula; nearly every other NP-completeness proof reduces from SAT or a problem already shown to reduce from it.

prompt: Proving HAM-PATH ∈ NP: which condition on the certificate p = (v_1, ..., v_n) costs O(V²) to verify, making it the bottleneck of the O(V²) total verification time?
options: Checking that all vertices in p are pairwise distinct (no repeats)
Checking that p has the correct number of vertices
Checking that every v_i is a vertex of G
Checking that consecutive pairs (v_i, v_{i+1}) are edges of G
explanation: Distinctness requires comparing up to O(V²) pairs of vertices in the worst case; the other three checks are each a single O(V) pass over the certificate.

prompt: Why can the Hamiltonian Path problem be solved in polynomial time when restricted to directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), even though the general problem is NP-complete?
options: In a DAG, any Hamiltonian path must follow the (unique) topological order, collapsing the exponential search space to exactly one candidate to check
DAGs never have a Hamiltonian path, so the answer is trivially always 'no'
DAGs allow negative-weight edges, which speeds up the search
The NP-completeness proof for general graphs doesn't actually apply to any graphs, so this isn't a real restriction
explanation: A path can't go backward against a DAG's edge directions without revisiting a vertex, so it must respect topological order — checking whether that one specific order is actually a valid path (each consecutive pair an edge) takes only O(V+E) via topological sort plus O(V) verification.
